questions.question:
**Select the antonym of the given word.**

Attract
questions.solution:
The correct answer is '**Repel**'. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ​The word ‘**Attract**’(verb) means- "to cause somebody/something to go to something or give attention to something". (आकर्षित करना; आकृष्‍ट करना; लुभाना)

 
 
• E.g.* These flowers are brightly coloured in order to **attract **butterflies.*
 
 *​*Let’s have a look at the meaning of the words that are given in the options:

 
 
• **Lure**(verb)- “to persuade or trick somebody to go somewhere or do something, usually by offering him/her something nice”. (प्रलोभन देकर किसी को धोखे से कहीं ले जाना या कुछ करवाना)
 
• **Repel**(verb)- “to send or push somebody/something back or away”. (किसी व्‍यकि्त या वस्‍तु को पीछे या दूर भेज या धकेल देना)
 
• **Allure**(noun)- “the quality of being attractive and exciting”. (प्रलोभन, आकर्षण)
 
• **Invite**(verb)- “to ask somebody to come somewhere or to do something”. (किसी को कहीं आने या कुछ करने के लिए कहना, निमंत्रित करना)
 
 
 
• Therefore, as per the points mentioned above, we find that ‘Repel’ is the correct antonym for the given bold word.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• *​*The antonyms of the given word 'Attract' are- 'Repel', '**disgust**', '**refuse**', 'reject', '**dissuade**', etc.
 
• The synonyms of the given word 'Attract' are- '**captivate**', '**entice**', '**allure**', '**interest**', etc.
 
• Example of 'Attract' in a sentence__: 
 
 
• *The mud flats **attract **large numbers of birds.*

questions.question:
Identify the segment in the sentence which contains the grammatical error from the given options. 

Put off the air conditioner unless you will catch a cold
questions.solution:
The correct solution is option 4.

'unless' is grammatically incorrect because it means except if. 

The most appropriate substitution to be used here is *or else, *which is used to say what will happen if another thing does not happen.

Example: *We must be there by three, or else we'll miss the beginning of the show*.

__Correct sentence:__ *Put off the air conditioner, **or else** you will catch a cold*

The bodies _____ identiﬁed as those of two suspected drug dealers.
questions.solution:
The correct solution is option 2.

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select option 'No substitution required'.**

The interview __was broadcast__ on the same day he was sworn in as President.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'Option 2'** i.e.** 'No substitution required'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence uses the verb "**broadcast"** in the passive voice correctly, which is "was broadcast." This is the correct form for referring to an event in the passive voice in the past.
 
• **"Broadcast" **is both the past and present form of the verb, unlike other verbs that typically end in -ed for their past forms. Thus, **"was broadcast" **is correct.
 
• The context of the sentence does not require a perfect tense ("had broadcast") because it clearly states that the interview was broadcast on the same day he was sworn in. There is no need to emphasize the sequence of events.
 
• The sentence is **grammatically correct **and conveys the message clearly and effectively without any ambiguity.
 
• Using **"broadcast" **in this construction is correct and aligns with standard English usage for referring to events transmitted on television, radio, or other broadcasting mediums.

Therefore, the **correct answer** is- **No substitution required.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1, "had broadcast,"** introduces the past perfect tense, which is unnecessary here since the action's timing relative to another event is already clear.
 
• **Option 3, "was broadcasted,"** is a common mistake. "Broadcasted" as the past form is less preferred; the standard past simple and past participle form is "broadcast."
 
• **Option 4, "broadcast"** without any auxiliary verb would shift the sentence to the present tense or suggest an imperative mood, which does not fit the context of a past event being described.
